books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: House vote on the Wilmot Proviso, August 1846, as tabulated in Princeton Review, Chapter 9. The table is drawn from the book's account of the vote.
stimulus.text:
How the House of Representatives voted on the Wilmot Proviso in August 1846, by section and by party:

| Members | Whigs | Democrats |
|---|---|---|
| Northern | all in favor | all but four in favor |
| Southern | all but two opposed | all opposed |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Wilmot Proviso, which the House was voting on, would have done which of the following?

options.text: Banned slavery in any territory the United States acquired from Mexico.
Admitted California as a free state immediately.
options.misconception: California did not become a state until 1850, and the Proviso was about all territory from Mexico, not California alone.

options.text: Extended the Missouri Compromise line of 36°30′ to the Pacific Ocean.
options.misconception: Extending the Missouri Compromise line was Polk's own proposal; the Proviso banned slavery outright in the new lands.

options.text: Allowed the settlers of each new territory to vote on whether to permit slavery.
options.misconception: Letting settlers vote was popular sovereignty, a later idea; the Proviso was a flat ban by Congress.

rationales.A: The Proviso said slavery “shall never exist” in any territory acquired from Mexico.
rationales.B: California's statehood came in 1850 under the Compromise; the Proviso covered all the land from Mexico.
rationales.C: Polk proposed extending the Missouri Compromise line; Wilmot proposed a total ban instead.
rationales.D: Popular sovereignty let settlers decide; the Proviso left them no choice at all.
rationales.general:
1. Go back to Wilmot's words: no slavery “in any part of said territory” taken from Mexico.
2. Notice how absolute that is. It bans slavery everywhere in the new lands, not just north of a line.
3. That is why the vote split by section: the ban threatened the South's whole future in the West.
Remember: the Proviso was a ban, not a line and not a vote — and its bluntness is what made it explosive.
